title: Texas governor's race, 45 days of posts

clusters.text: Dave Lowe, a lifelong Republican near a proposed Texas data center, says it is the first issue in his adult life he expects to affect him directly.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The CBS News "60 Minutes" transcript, "The data center uproar," has Lowe saying on air: "This is the first time in my adult life where there's been an issue that's come up that I feel like is going to directly impact me." 
It says he lives right by the proposed data center in Red Oak and told the reporters he's a lifelong conservative Republican.
 
The project is a Compass plan for 10 two-story data centers on rural agricultural land.
 Raw Story, IBTimes and WWAY report the same remark and the same "lifelong conservative Republican" description. The claim paraphrases the quote accurately, and it correctly presents it as Lowe's own statement. The "lifelong Republican" label comes from Lowe's self-description as relayed by CBS, and I found no independent check of it. That is a minor caveat, not a mismatch with the claim.

clusters.text: Gina Hinojosa will be an amazing governor for Texas.
A ReconMR/Siena poll has James Talarico at 48% and Ken Paxton at 44% in the Texas Senate race.
clusters.verdict_basis: ReconMR's own Texas Poll page and Siena Research Institute's release show the latest ReconMR/Siena result is Talarico 48%, Paxton 44%. The poll was fielded Oct 5–8 among 617 likely voters with a ±4.4 margin, per RealClearPolling, and released Oct 13. The Hill, Fox 7 Austin and Political Wire report the same figures. The wording "ReconMR/Siena" and both numbers are correct. One caveat on timing: the claim was first seen on Sept 9, before this poll was fielded. The earlier ReconMR/Siena poll (Sept 8–11) had Talarico ahead 49–43, and the October release describes 48–44 as down from that. So the figures were not accurate on Sept 9. They match the current poll, but a post dated Sept 9 could not have been citing it. The governor's-race context is not relevant to this Senate figure.

lanes.label: Abbott is solid and will win

clusters.text: A NYT/Siena poll of Texas likely voters finds Gina Hinojosa at 49% and Greg Abbott at 46%.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The NYT/Siena poll matches the claim. It was fielded Sept. 21–30 among 615 likely Texas voters and had Hinojosa at 49% and Abbott at 46%. 
Newsweek reports that Hinojosa moved ahead 49 to 46 among 615 likely voters when the Times/Siena returned to the field September 21-30.
 
Time reports the same figures.
 RealClearPolling's table also lists 
NY Times/Siena, 9/21 - 9/30, 615 LV, Abbott 46, Hinojosa 49.
 One caveat is timing. This poll was fielded after the claim's first-seen date of Sept. 17 and was released on a Saturday in early October (
CBS
). The previous NYT/Siena poll, in June, 
had Abbott ahead 51–44
. So the numbers could not have been published on Sept. 17, though the claim is accurate as a description of the poll now. Reports differ on the margin: some outlets say 3 points, which is the rounded gap, and the Hinojosa campaign says 4 points. The claim states no margin, so this doesn't affect it.

lanes.label: Abbott is solid and will win

clusters.text: Greg Abbott pledges to fully ban Sharia law in Texas without waiting for Washington.
clusters.verdict_basis: Dallas Fox affiliate coverage, reproduced by Joe.My.God, reports that Abbott spoke on the second night of the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, on Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026. It quotes him saying, "We are not waiting on Washington, D.C." and "We will fully ban Sharia Law in Texas." The Houston Chronicle and a Concho Valley Homepage report also say he vowed at the Dallas convention to "fully ban" Sharia law in Texas. This matches the claim's wording, date and attribution. I did not find a video or transcript of the speech, so the quote rests on secondary reporting. The pledge also fits his earlier statements. On Mar. 4, 2026 he posted that Sharia law would be "completely banned in Texas this next session." Context the claim leaves out: Abbott and others describe Texas as already banning Sharia law, and a 2025 law (HB 4211) targets "Sharia compounds." Legal experts quoted in coverage also say the First Amendment limits what a ban could do. These points concern whether the pledge can be carried out, not whether he made it.

lanes.label: Abbott is solid and will win

clusters.text: A Republican internal poll in Texas Senate District 9 has Gina Hinojosa ahead of Greg Abbott 49% to 40%.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Quorum Report published the poll on Sept. 21, 2026. It described it as 
a Republican poll of Tarrant County voters
 from a GOP pollster. Mediaite reported that it had 
Hinojosa over Abbott 49 to 40
. Mediaite and Yahoo/Tarrant coverage tied the poll to SD9. Mediaite said it was conducted Sept. 10–15 among 600 likely voters, with a ±3 margin of error. The Yahoo/Tarrant report said it covered 
600 likely Senate District 9 voters
. The claim's numbers, district and partisan source all match. Two caveats apply. The pollster was never named and no polling memo was published, because Quorum Report described the source only as 
"a reputable Republican pollster"
. The result is also a single-district sample, not a statewide result. It is not evidence that Hinojosa leads statewide, where public polls show a close race. I did not see the Quorum Report article's full text, so the 49–40 figure rests on Mediaite's report of it.

clusters.text: A Recon MR/Siena poll of 614 Texas likely voters finds Gina Hinojosa at 49% and Greg Abbott at 45%.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim matches the record. KXAN/Nexstar reported that the ReconMR/Siena poll 
shows Hinojosa leading Abbott by four points, 49% to 45%
. The same report says 
it surveyed 614 likely voters with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.3 percentage points
. The UT Austin Texas Politics Project poll tracker and RealClearPolling both list the Sept. 8–11 ReconMR poll as 614 likely voters, Abbott 45 and Hinojosa 49. The poll was released Sept. 17, which fits the date the claim was first seen. A later ReconMR/Siena poll (Oct. 5–8, 617 likely voters) had 
Abbott ahead 48% to 47%
. That is a different poll and does not affect the accuracy of the September figures.

clusters.text: An AARP poll by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research of Texas likely voters finds Greg Abbott at 49% and Gina Hinojosa at 46%.
clusters.verdict_basis: Basis: AARP's own release (Sept. 10, 2026) and its research page report a Texas survey of 895 likely voters. The survey was fielded Aug. 30–Sept. 1 by Fabrizio Ward (R) and Impact Research (D). The governor's race result is Abbott 49%, Hinojosa 46%, a 3-point Abbott lead. The UT Texas Politics Project poll tracker lists the same figures (49–46) for the AARP survey. The claim's pollsters, population, candidates and numbers all match the primary source. Another blog post cites a 47–47 tie, but that appears to come from a different poll and doesn't contradict the AARP figures.

lanes.label: Abbott is solid and will win

clusters.text: Republicans have led Texas for more than three decades.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Reporting consistently says no Democrat has won statewide office in Texas since 1994, and that Republicans have held every statewide office since then. 
AP, carried by PBS, called it the longest losing streak in the nation.
 The Hill, in current coverage of the 2026 races, repeats that 
no Democrat has won statewide since 1994
. The governor's office is the clearest case. 
George W. Bush beat Ann Richards in the 1994 gubernatorial election
, and 
Richards, elected in 1990, was the last Texas Democratic governor
. That puts Republican control of the governorship at roughly 31 years as of September 2026. KXAN also describes it as 
"the past three decades"
 of Republican dominance. The claim is vague about what "led" means. It holds for statewide offices and the governorship, which is the natural reading, though I did not check the dates when Republicans took control of each legislative chamber.

clusters.text: Texas Republicans have had decades in power and have no credibility promising to fix problems they have not fixed.
Texas is refusing to release its maternal death report until after the midterm vote.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The timing is accurate. The Texas Tribune, via 
KSAT, reports the biennial report was due Sept. 1 and has been pushed to December
. 
That puts the release after the Nov. 3 election
. The Tribune also notes 
this is the second time since 2013 that the review has come out only after a midterm
. The wording "refusing" is the weak point. A DSHS spokesperson said the report 
is not "delayed" and is going through an internal review process
. DSHS says the acting commissioner asked the committee to strengthen it, and it cites 
a 2025 provision in HB 4666 allowing reports to be submitted by Dec. 1
. The Texas Observer says that law 
allows but does not require a December 1 submission, so the committee could have kept its September deadline
. The bill's author called the coincidence hard to believe but 
said she can't say whether the amendment was meant to push the report past the election
. Advocates and Rep. Crockett asked for release before the election, and 
that call has gone unmet
. I found no primary record showing the election was the reason, and the claim implies that motive.

clusters.text: Ectopic pregnancy deaths rose faster in states with abortion bans.
clusters.verdict_basis:
A ProPublica analysis of CDC WONDER data, published Sept. 9, 2026, found that ectopic pregnancy deaths rose nationwide. 
The climb was much steeper in states that banned abortion after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022.
 For 2023–2025, 
the rate was 13.1 per million live births in states with bans beginning at six weeks or earlier, compared with 7.1 in states without bans.
 NPR's interview with the reporter repeats the finding that 
the rise is steeper in states that implemented an abortion ban after Dobbs.
 The claim describes a difference in how fast deaths rose, and it does not say bans caused it. As worded, it matches the data. The caveats are that 
researchers cautioned the data do not prove abortion bans caused the increase
, and that 
states that later banned abortion already had higher mortality in 2014
. The reporting also notes that 
COVID-era hospital chaos likely contributed to some deaths
. Counts are small, which is why the data are grouped into three-year intervals. A reader could take the claim to imply causation, which the sources do not establish. I did not look at the underlying CDC data directly, only at ProPublica's analysis and reporting on it.

clusters.text: An NPR/Marist poll of Texas registered voters finds Gina Hinojosa at 49% and Greg Abbott at 46%.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The Marist Poll's own release covers interviews from Sept. 17–20, 2026 with 1,139 Texas registered voters and a ±4.4-point margin of error. 
It says 3 points separate Hinojosa (49%) and Abbott (46%) among Texas registered voters.
 
Mediaite reports the same figures, with 1% for another candidate and 3% undecided.
 The UT Texas Politics Project tracker lists this poll as 
"NPR/Marist"
 with the same 46/49 split. The "NPR" label comes from that tracker and from Hinojosa's campaign release. The Marist page text I retrieved doesn't mention NPR, and The Hill and Mediaite call it a "Marist" poll. The numbers, the voter population and the date all match the claim.

   The claim describes the September poll, so it holds up as worded. A later Marist poll is a different survey. 
It found Hinojosa trailing Abbott by 4 points among likely voters.
 The September lead is also within the margin of error.

clusters.text: An NPR/Marist poll finds James Talarico at 50% and Ken Paxton at 44% in the Texas Senate race.
clusters.verdict_basis: Marist's own release of its September 2026 Texas poll reports Talarico at 50% and Paxton at 44% among registered voters. The poll was conducted Sept. 17–20 with n=1,139 and a margin of error of ±4.4 points. The UT Texas Politics Project poll tracker lists the same NPR/Marist result (Paxton 44, Talarico 50) and says it was added on Sept. 23, the day the claim first appeared on X. A newer Marist poll, released around Oct. 14, is closer. The Hill and Forbes put it at 47–45 among likely voters, and a Yahoo report cites 48–44 among registered voters. That makes the 50–44 figure the September result and not the current one. The claim's numbers, pollster and race are all correct for the poll it describes, so I rate it supported. The claim doesn't say the sample is registered voters, and the 6-point lead is within the stated margin of error.

clusters.text: Greg Abbott is deploying the Texas Department of Public Safety to root out Sharia courts anywhere in Texas.
clusters.verdict_basis:
On Nov. 19, 2025, 
Abbott sent a letter to North Texas district attorneys and sheriffs, the Attorney General and DPS, alerting them to possible criminal violations by Sharia tribunals and calling for investigations
 (gov.texas.gov). DPS was one of several recipients, and the letter named entities 
"including in Collin and Dallas counties"
, chiefly the Dallas-based Islamic Tribunal. It was a request to investigate, not a DPS deployment. The Center Square, by contrast, described it as a direction to investigate the tribunal and "potentially other entities." Separately, on Nov. 20, 
Abbott directed DPS to launch criminal investigations into the Muslim Brotherhood and CAIR
. The governor's release adds that 
"We will also focus on individuals or groups who unlawfully impose Sharia law"
, and says 
DPS agents on FBI Joint Terrorism Task Forces around the state
 will gather intelligence. That DPS order is aimed at those two groups, with Sharia enforcement as an added focus. So there is a real basis for the gist: Abbott has pointed DPS at alleged Sharia courts and at groups that impose Sharia law. But the claim presents a present-tense, statewide DPS operation targeting "Sharia courts an

lanes.label: Abbott is solid and will win

clusters.text: Taxes in Texas are higher under Greg Abbott.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim is true only if "higher" means more total dollars collected, and that is a narrow reading of it. Comptroller-based figures show that 
property taxes totaled $52.2 billion in 2015 and an estimated $73 billion in 2021
. A later analysis, which used levy data from the same comptroller, put 
total levies at $49.11 billion in 2014 and $89.45 billion in 2025, an 82% rise
. That is the basis for Hinojosa's "85%" line. However, 
the same analysis shows property values rose 125% over those years
, and it found that the 
levy per $100 of market value fell from about $1.95 to about $1.58
. That analysis comes from a newsletter, so treat it as secondary. The Texas Tribune reported that 
the typical Texas homeowner paid less in property taxes last year than just before the pandemic, per Census Bureau data
. It also reported that 
city and county taxes have kept growing
, and that Abbott's own framing is that local governments are offsetting state relief. PolitiFact has noted that 
property taxes are set locally, so the governor's role is indirect
. The claim also covers only property taxes in practice. I found no source on Texas's overall tax burden or other taxes, so the claim as wor

clusters.text: The same Republican internal poll has Democrat Taylor Rehmet leading Republican Leigh Wambsganss 53% to 39% in Texas Senate District 9.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Quorum Report published the poll on Sept. 21, 2026. Its headline describes 
a Republican poll of Tarrant County voters showing Sen. Rehmet with a commanding lead over GOP challenger Wambsganss
. Mediaite's write-up of that poll gives the figures: 
Democrat incumbent State Sen. Rehmet over Republican Wambsganss, challenging him again, 53 to 39
. The same poll has 
Hinojosa over Abbott 49 to 40
, so "the same poll" is accurate. The numbers, the candidates and the district match. Two caveats: the pollster is not named in the coverage I found, and I could only see the Quorum Report page in part, so I'm relying on Mediaite for the exact 53–39 figure. The poll is also a single GOP-sourced survey, not a public one.

clusters.text: A NYT/Siena poll finds James Talarico at 51% and Ken Paxton at 45% in the Texas Senate race.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The numbers match a real poll. Fox 7 Austin and RealClearPolling report a New York Times/Siena poll of 615 likely voters, fielded Sept. 21–30, 2026, with Talarico at 51% and Paxton at 45%. Newsweek and Forbes report the same figures. The timing is the problem. That poll was fielded after the claim was first seen on X (Sept. 2) and was reported in early October. The only earlier Times/Siena Texas poll, from June 19–27, had the two tied at 47–47 (
Siena Research Institute
, and 
Fox 7 says the two were tied at 47% in June
). So on Sept. 2 no Times/Siena poll showed 51–45. The figures are accurate for the later poll, but the claim as first posted could not have reflected an existing Times/Siena result. That makes it misleading as posted, though it is accurate now. Also, the claim's context is the governor's race, but the figures concern the Senate race. The claim does say "Senate race," so that part is consistent.

clusters.text: A photo of Indian Americans in overalls and burnt orange shows people from anywhere can become as American as white people.
A UT/Texas Politics Project poll finds Gina Hinojosa narrowly ahead of Greg Abbott, 49% to 48%.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The UT/Texas Politics Project's own release on its latest poll reports 
Hinojosa holding a statistically insignificant one-point lead over the incumbent, 49% to 48%, with 3% preferring "someone else"
. KXAN reports the same figures and says 
the poll of 1,200 registered Texas voters was conducted Sept. 25 through Oct. 5, with a margin of error of +/- 2.83 points
. The 49–48 figure applies to likely voters (
49% support among likely voters, compared with 48% for Abbott
). The Texas Tribune and Houston Chronicle also report it, and the Tribune calls it 
effectively a tie
. "Narrowly ahead" is therefore accurate, though the lead is well inside the margin of error. The earlier UT/TPP poll in August had Abbott ahead 45–40, so this is a new result. A separate Marist poll showed Abbott ahead, which doesn't affect what this claim says about the UT/TPP poll.

clusters.text: People should follow Gina Hinojosa on social media.
The Texas governor's race has swung 10 points toward Gina Hinojosa since June.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The 10-point figure comes from one poll, not from the race as a whole. The NYT/Siena poll had Abbott ahead 51–44 in June. Its Sept. 21–30 poll had Hinojosa ahead 49–46 (
Newsweek
), which is a 10-point swing in margin. Hinojosa's campaign release uses the same "10-point swing" wording for that poll alone (
ginafortexas.com
). Other pollsters show smaller shifts. In the UT/Texas Politics Project poll, 
Abbott led by 7 in early June
, but the October UT poll has 
Hinojosa up 49–48
, an 8-point change. ReconMR went from 
Abbott +6 in June
 to Hinojosa +4 in September, but its Oct. 8 poll (published Oct. 13) 
put Abbott back ahead
 at 48–47. The latest RealClearPolling average is 
Abbott +2.2
, and its recent polls include Marist with Abbott +4 (Oct. 8–11). Describing "the race" as having swung 10 points since June overstates what most polls and the averages show. It is accurate only for the NYT/Siena comparison, and that comparison uses rounded toplines.

clusters.text: A YouGov/Univision poll of registered voters has Greg Abbott and Gina Hinojosa tied at 47%.
clusters.verdict_basis:
- The claim matches the poll record. 
The N+ Univision poll released Sept. 9 showed both candidates tied at 47% with 5% undecided.
 
It was conducted Aug. 27 to Sept. 4 and surveyed 1,000 registered voters.
 The margin of error was 
plus or minus 3.6 percentage points
.
- Newsweek and RealClearPolling's poll table list the same poll as a 47–47 tie among registered voters. The pollster is given as YouGov or as Univision, and the poll's name is given as "N+ Univision/YouGov".
- Hinojosa's campaign also publicized the poll. Fox 7 Austin's report names the poll as "N+ Univision".
- The claim doesn't say the poll is current. Later polls differ, for example a separate YouGov poll of likely voters (Sept. 28–Oct. 5) that had Hinojosa ahead 48–47. That doesn't change what this poll found.

clusters.text: In recorded audio, Ken Paxton said Greg Abbott is struggling in his reelection bid.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Rolling Stone published audio from a Sept. 24 private fundraiser in Washington, D.C. 
In the audio, Paxton says "Yes, Abbott is struggling."
 
He adds that the race is "still close" even though Abbott has name ID and money advantages over Hinojosa.
 Mediaite, Newsweek, Raw Story and the San Antonio Current report the same quote. 
In a second exchange Paxton says Abbott is "struggling, but he has a lot of money."
 The claim matches the reporting. Two caveats: the recording was made privately by an attendee and leaked, and I did not hear the audio myself, so I'm relying on outlets quoting it. 
Paxton's spokesperson called it "cherry-picked audio" and a partisan hit job.
 The spokesperson's statement, as quoted, does not dispute that Paxton said it.

clusters.text: Greg Abbott released a video about his recent trip to Israel.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Abbott's office has published videos about Israel trips, but the records I found don't show a recent one. A governor's office press release dated Jan. 26, 2016 says it 
released a web video highlighting the Governor's recent trip to Israel and Switzerland
. The Nov. 2023 trip was his third, according to 
CBS Texas
. His office's Nov. 3, 2023 release said 
video of Governor Abbott and Governor Stitt's visit to Israel is available
. In an Oct. 2025 release, Abbott 
spoke of his trip to Israel just weeks after the October 7, 2023 attack
, which suggests no newer trip by then. I found no reporting or official record of an Israel trip in 2026 or of a related video around Sept. 2026. A Texas Border Business page carries an "Aug 3, 2026" date, but its text is the 2023 trip announcement, so that date looks like a page-date artifact. The claim as worded ("recent trip") fits the 2016 video and, loosely, the 2023 trip video, so it is out of date or misleading. It is not supported as a description of anything current. This rests on web searches only. I did not check Abbott's own social accounts for September 2026.

clusters.text: In NYT/Siena polling, Greg Abbott led Gina Hinojosa 51% to 44% in June, but Hinojosa led 49% to 46% in September.
clusters.verdict_basis:
RealClearPolling's poll table lists two NYT/Siena Texas governor polls. 
The June poll ran 6/19–6/27 among 656 likely voters and had Abbott at 51.
 Its table gives Hinojosa 44 for June, a 7-point Abbott lead. 
The 9/21–9/30 poll of 615 likely voters has Abbott 46 and Hinojosa 49, a 3-point Hinojosa lead.
 Newsweek reports the same figures: 
June 51–44 for Abbott, then 49–46 for Hinojosa when Times/Siena returned to the field September 21–30.
 Time confirms the September 49–46 result. Some coverage calls the September lead "four points," but that comes from unrounded vote shares. The claim uses the rounded toplines, which match the records, and it says "September" without naming a specific poll, which is accurate for the Sept. 21–30 survey.

clusters.text: Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton are enriching themselves and their billionaire friends at Texans' expense.
Texans' electricity bills have skyrocketed.
clusters.verdict_basis: Electricity costs in Texas have risen, but the data doesn't clearly show a "skyrocketing" recent surge. The Houston Chronicle reported a Texas Energy Poverty Research Institute (TEPRI) analysis. It found residential prices up about 30% since 2021, which adds roughly $35–40 a month to the average bill. It also noted that Texas rates remain below the national average. EIA-based figures compiled by Energy Factbook show Texas residential rates at 15.88¢/kWh in July 2026. That is up 3.4% over 12 months, 13.8% over 3 years and 35.4% over 5 years. Powerplans, also using EIA data, puts the 2025 average bill at $173 a month, up 5.7% from 2024. Those are mostly aggregator and advocacy-group compilations, not primary EIA or PUC records. Rates have climbed notably since 2020, and some individual bills are very high (KLTV). The 2026 year-on-year increases are modest, and some trackers show rates easing in mid-2026 (ElectricityPlans). So the claim is directionally defensible, but "skyrocketed" overstates the recent trend. The claim also offers no timeframe, and the $40-a-month figure Hinojosa's campaign uses is attributed to Abbott's tenure, which is a causal framing.

clusters.text: The ERCOT board, appointed by Greg Abbott, gave itself a 30% raise.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The raise happened. The Texas Tribune reported that 
board members approved a raise for themselves that would result in an average annual pay of $219,375, a 30% increase from the previous average of $169,375, according to board documents.
 Per the Tribune, 
the increase comes from a $150,000 "retention award" paid at the end of each director's three-year term
. 
The vote was unanimous, though board chair Bill Flores abstained.
 The "appointed by Greg Abbott" part is wrong as worded. Under SB 2, 
a three-member Selection Committee picks the eight selected directors. Its members are appointed one each by the governor, the lieutenant governor and the House speaker.
 The Tribune likewise says 
board members are appointed by a committee of three people selected by the governor, the lieutenant governor and the House speaker.
 Abbott therefore appoints one of three selectors, not the board. The other four voting members are ex officio: 
the CEO, two PUC commissioners and the head of the Office of Public Utility Counsel, who are not getting the raises.
 The wording closely tracks a Hinojosa campaign statement calling them 
"Abbott's handpicked ERCOT board members"
. The reporting I found d

clusters.text: A UMass Lowell/YouGov poll of Texas likely voters finds Greg Abbott ahead of Gina Hinojosa, 48% to 44%.
clusters.verdict_basis:
UMass Lowell's Center for Public Opinion lists a UMass Lowell/YouGov poll of 850 likely Texas voters. 
It was conducted Sept. 18 to 28, with an adjusted margin of error of 4.5%.
 Political Wire reported that 
the poll finds Abbott (R) leading Hinojosa (D) 48% to 44%, with Pat Dixon (L) at 1%.
 Newsweek gave the same figures and added that 
Abbott's lead is within the margin of error.
 Later Newsweek and Yahoo/Austin-area poll roundups still list the UMass Lowell result as Abbott 48%, Hinojosa 44%.

The claim's numbers, pollster, and population (likely voters) all match. The poll was published around Oct. 8, two days after the claim was first seen on X (Oct. 6). The claim doesn't state a release date, so I did not treat that as an error. I could not open UMass Lowell's own release, only its poll index page. The figures come from Newsweek and Political Wire. Other polls cited in the same coverage show a closer race, and some show Hinojosa ahead. That doesn't change the accuracy of this claim.

lanes.label: Abbott is solid and will win

clusters.event: YouGov Texas poll: Talarico 50-44, Hinojosa 48-47
clusters.text: A YouGov poll finds Hispanic voters in Texas back Gina Hinojosa over Greg Abbott, 58% to 37%.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Newsweek reported on a YouGov survey of 3,622 likely voters, conducted Sept. 28 to Oct. 5, 2026. 
It had Hinojosa narrowly ahead of Abbott, 48% to 47%.
 The same report says 
Hinojosa leads Hispanic voters 58 percent to 37 percent
, which matches the claim's numbers and candidates. RealClearPolling lists the same poll with the same sample size, dates and topline (
Abbott 47, Hinojosa 48
), so the poll exists. I found the 58–37 crosstab only in Newsweek and did not find YouGov's own release. Other YouGov-branded polls give different Hispanic splits, such as 
51 to 43 in the UMass Lowell/YouGov poll
 and 
56–42 in the UT/YouGov poll
. The claim's figures match the Sept. 28–Oct. 5 poll specifically, so it holds as worded. Hispanic subgroups are small samples with wider margins of error than the 3-point topline.

clusters.text: Texas needs and is ready for a change in governor.
At least two Sharia courts are operating in the Dallas area.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The records name only one entity. Gov. Abbott's Nov. 19, 2025 letter said unnamed "entities" in Collin and Dallas counties "may be masquerading" as courts, and it singled out one group, the Islamic Tribunal in Dallas (
governor's office release
; 
KERA
). Paxton's April 2026 investigation also targets only that group (
AG release
). I found no public record or news report that identifies a second Sharia court in the Dallas area. 
As of Sept. 19, 2026, the Paxton investigation had produced no public finding
, so nothing official has confirmed even one illegal "court." The Tribunal says 
it does not function as a court of law and does not issue legally binding judgments
. Snopes and PolitiFact have described it as a voluntary, nonbinding mediation and arbitration forum. The plural in Abbott's letter is the only basis I found for "two," and it names no second entity.

lanes.label: Abbott is solid and will win

clusters.text: The Texas Constitution does not allow Sharia courts or Sharia law.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The wording matches what Abbott said on Hannity in November 2025 (
Fox News video, Nov. 20, 2025
), so the attribution is not the problem. His related Nov. 19 letter to prosecutors did not cite a specific constitutional provision. It 
relied on the Texas Penal Code, saying a tribunal that holds itself out as a binding "court" masquerades as a rival court
. It also 
said the Constitution's religious protections give religious courts no authority to skirt state and federal laws
. The Texas Constitution itself doesn't name Sharia. Reporting and policy analysis say religious arbitration is not prohibited. 
Individuals may resolve disputes by religious principles if they stay within contract law and public policy
. 
Courts can enforce valid arbitration awards from such panels, as they can with other private arbitration
. The Islamic Tribunal says 
it only handles mediation and arbitration in family disputes and refers final rulings to Texas courts
. Paxton's April 2026 probe is aimed at whether it falsely claimed state-court authority (
The Conversation
). No court has ruled on this.

clusters.text: Kalshi's market gives Greg Abbott a 78% chance of winning and Gina Hinojosa 22%.
clusters.verdict_basis:
